pedagogy.summary: Thousandths continue the tenfold nesting one place further: split a hundredth into ten and each piece is a thousandth, so 1/100 ÷ 10 = 1/1000, and the places march ones → tenths → hundredths → thousandths, each a tenth of the one before. The coordinating facts are 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth, 100 thousandths = 1 tenth, and 1000 thousandths = 1 whole. In notation, 25 thousandths is 25/1000 = 0.025, where the leading placeholder zero holds the empty tenths place. The recurring obstacle is again whole-number bias — believing a thousandth is bigger than a hundredth 'because 1000 > 100' — and the placeholder error 25/1000 → 0.25. Build thousandths by repeated ÷10 subdivision and by zooming in on the number line between two hundredths.
bestPractices: Derive thousandths by subdividing a hundredth into ten, making 1/100 ÷ 10 = 1/1000 an action the child performs, so the recursive tenfold structure is felt rather than told.
Coordinate two levels of nesting explicitly: 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth AND 100 thousandths = 1 tenth, so children compose the ×10 steps instead of applying a single one.
Zoom the number line: locate 0.345 by zooming between 0.34 and 0.35 and splitting into ten, so a thousandth is seen as a tenth of the gap between hundredths.
Drill the placeholder in notation: 25/1000 = 0.025 (two leading places filled), contrasting 25/100 = 0.25 and 25/10 = 2.5, so place governs the number of zeros.
Confront whole-number bias directly — compare 0.05 and 0.005, or one hundredth against one thousandth — so 'more parts, smaller each' overturns 'bigger denominator, bigger part'.
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart: ones | tenths | hundredths | thousandths
Number line with zoom between two hundredths, split into ten thousandths
Recursive subdivision model (whole → tenth → hundredth → thousandth, ten-for-one each step)
Comparison pair 0.05 vs 0.005 to break whole-number bias
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias: a thousandth taken as bigger than a hundredth or tenth 'because 1000 > 100'.
Placeholder error: writing 25 thousandths as 0.25 (or 0.0025), not 0.025.
Miscoordinating the nesting: saying 10 thousandths = 1 tenth (one ×10 step) instead of 100 thousandths = 1 tenth.
Treating the digits after the point as a whole number, so 0.025 is read as 'twenty-five' and mis-sized.
Thinking the number line 'runs out' at hundredths, so not subdividing further to place a thousandth.

learn.summary: Thousandths continue the tenfold nesting one place further: split a hundredth into ten and each piece is a thousandth, so 1/100 ÷ 10 = 1/1000, and the places march ones → tenths → hundredths → thousandths, each a tenth of the one before. The coordinating facts are 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth, 100 thousandths = 1 tenth, and 1000 thousandths = 1 whole. In notation, 25 thousandths = 25/1000 = 0.025, where the leading placeholder zero holds the empty tenths place. The recurring obstacles are whole-number bias (believing a thousandth is bigger than a hundredth 'because 1000 > 100') and the placeholder error (writing 25/1000 as 0.25). Build thousandths by repeated ÷10 subdivision and by zooming in on the number line between two hundredths.

activities.title: Zoom the number line to place 0.345
feedback: If a learner says the line stops at hundredths, prompt: 'The gap between 0.34 and 0.35 can itself be cut into ten — what is each new piece called?'
If they place 0.345 at the wrong mark, have them count the ten equal steps aloud and check that 0.345 sits on the fifth mark (5 thousandths past 0.34).
If a learner thinks a thousandth is the smallest piece possible, invite them to split it into ten again and name the ten-thousandth, reinforcing that the ÷10 subdivision can always continue.
Confirm success when they can name each step as one thousandth and justify the position of 0.345 by counting thousandths.
activities.rationale: Locating a thousandth by zooming between two hundredths and subdividing into ten makes the recursive tenfold structure an action the child performs, rather than a rule stated to them. If a live number line is used, dragging a zoom control and watching the gap split into ten labelled steps makes the mechanism concrete; a drawn paper number line zoomed and re-divided on a fresh strip serves the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
Pupils should recognise and use thousandths and relate them to tenths, hundredths and decimal equivalents (Year 5 statutory content).
learnerActions: Start with a number line showing just 0.34 and 0.35, with nothing marked between them, and predict aloud roughly where 0.345 should go.
Zoom into the gap between 0.34 and 0.35 and divide it into ten equal steps; name what each single step is worth (one thousandth, a tenth of the gap between two hundredths).
Count the steps and place 0.345 exactly on the fifth mark (the midpoint of the gap), then state why: it is 5 thousandths past 0.34.
Repeat the zoom-and-split for another thousandth, e.g. place 0.347, so the subdivision becomes a repeatable action, not a one-off.
Extend the action one level further: split a single thousandth into ten equal parts and name each tinier piece a ten-thousandth, illustrating that the ÷10 subdivision can always be repeated again.
activities.intendedInsight: A thousandth is a tenth of the gap between two hundredths; the number line never 'runs out' — you can always subdivide one more time by ten to locate a finer value (a tenth of a thousandth is a ten-thousandth).

activities.title: Split a hundredth and compare sizes to break whole-number bias
feedback: If the learner predicts the thousandth is bigger 'because 1000 beats 100', do not just correct — have them physically lay one thousandth against one hundredth so the size difference is visible, then restate the rule 'more parts means each is smaller'.
For 0.05 vs 0.005, if they pick 0.005, point to the split: 0.005 is 5 thousandths while 0.05 is 50 thousandths (ten times larger); have them count how many thousandths are in each.
Confirm success when the learner states that a thousandth is smaller than a hundredth and can explain why the larger number 1000 does not make the part larger.
activities.rationale: Directly predicting, then confronting the prediction with a visible length comparison, targets whole-number bias in the moment the child commits to a wrong reason. Showing one thousandth beside one hundredth makes 'more parts, smaller each' concrete; a live splitter that recolours or relabels each new piece, or a paper strip cut into ten, both make the subdivision tangible. A paper strip cut into ten has slight thickness, so treat it as a model of the ideal zero-thickness partition, not identical to it.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
learnerActions: Before comparing, predict which is bigger, one hundredth or one thousandth, and say WHY in words.
Take one hundredth and split it into ten equal parts; identify each part as one thousandth.
Lay a single thousandth beside a whole hundredth and describe what you see — the thousandth is tiny next to the hundredth.
Reconcile this with your prediction: even though 1000 is a bigger number than 100, a thousandth is a smaller amount because it comes from cutting into more, smaller parts.
Compare 0.05 and 0.005 directly and state which is bigger and why, when both use the digit 5.
activities.intendedInsight: More, smaller parts means each part is smaller: a thousandth is smaller than a hundredth despite 1000 > 100, overturning 'bigger denominator, bigger part'.

activities.title: Write thousandths and justify the placeholder zero
feedback: If the learner writes 0.25 for 25 thousandths, return to the chart: thousandths is the third place after the point, so 25 must occupy hundredths and thousandths, leaving tenths empty and needing a 0.
If they write 0.0025, check column by column: the 5 should sit in thousandths (third place), not further right.
Confirm success when they both write 0.025 correctly and explain, using the chart, why the zero after the point is needed and why 25/100 and 25/1000 differ.
activities.rationale: Writing thousandths within an explicit place-value chart and contrasting 25/10, 25/100, 25/1000 makes the placeholder error visible and correctable by reasoning about place rather than digit-copying. A running chart that updates as the learner fills each column, or a hand-drawn chart, both make the empty tenths cell explicit.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
Pupils should recognise and use thousandths and relate them to tenths, hundredths and decimal equivalents (Year 5 statutory content).
learnerActions: Using a place-value chart with columns ones | tenths | hundredths | thousandths, write 25 thousandths: place the 2 in hundredths and the 5 in thousandths.
Fill the empty tenths column with a 0 and write the decimal 0.025, then explain that the zero holds the empty tenths place.
Contrast the set 25/10 = 2.5, 25/100 = 0.25, 25/1000 = 0.025, and describe how the place of the value decides where the digits land and how many leading places are filled.
Write a second example, e.g. 35 thousandths = 35/1000 = 0.035, and say why there is one placeholder zero straight after the decimal point (in the tenths place).
activities.intendedInsight: The place a value occupies, not just the digits, fixes the written decimal; the placeholder zero in 0.025 holds the empty tenths position so the 2 lands in hundredths and the 5 in thousandths.

activities.title: Compose two tenfold steps: 10 and 100 thousandths
feedback: If the learner says 10 thousandths = 1 tenth, build it in stages: 'How many thousandths in a hundredth? And how many hundredths in a tenth? So how many thousandths in a tenth?'
Have them count on a subdivided line through both levels to see the two steps accumulate to 100.
Confirm success when they answer 100 thousandths per tenth and can name both tenfold steps that compose it.
activities.rationale: Explicitly coordinating two levels of nesting addresses the miscoordination error (saying 10 rather than 100 thousandths per tenth) by having the child compose the steps instead of applying one. Counting through the levels on a subdivided line or stacking the facts on a chart both make the two steps visible.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
Pupils should recognise and use thousandths and relate them to tenths, hundredths and decimal equivalents (Year 5 statutory content).
learnerActions: State and show that 10 thousandths make 1 hundredth (one ÷10 subdivision).
Then show that 10 hundredths make 1 tenth, so composing the two steps gives 100 thousandths = 1 tenth.
Continue the chain to 1000 thousandths = 1 whole, naming each tenfold step.
Answer the trap question 'How many thousandths are in one tenth?' and justify 100 (two tenfold steps), explaining why 10 is wrong (it skips a step).
activities.intendedInsight: Getting from thousandths to tenths is two tenfold steps, not one: 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth and 100 thousandths = 1 tenth; the nesting composes rather than applying a single ×10.

activities.title: Check and diagnose with targeted questions
feedback: For the comparison item, if the learner selects 0.005 citing 1000 > 100, route back to the split-and-compare activity to re-establish 'more parts, smaller each'.
For 25/1000, if they omit the placeholder zero, return to the place-value chart activity.
Treat the 'why' answers as diagnostic: a learner who answers correctly but cannot explain the two-step nesting or the placeholder still needs the composing and notation activities.
activities.rationale: These checkable items with distractors (the 1000 > 100 comparison, the missing placeholder) surface whole-number bias and placeholder errors diagnostically. Checks assess outcomes rather than build the nesting insight, so they complement, not replace, the subdivision and zoom activities.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
learnerActions: Complete 25/1000 = 0.0__ and justify where the 2 and 5 sit and why the zero is there.
Complete '100 thousandths = __ tenth' and explain the two-step reasoning.
Decide which is bigger, 0.05 or 0.005, and give a reason that does not rely on 'more digits means bigger'.
Place 0.345 between 0.34 and 0.35 by stating how many equal steps are in the gap and which step 0.345 is.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct answers plus a stated reason distinguish genuine grasp of the recursive tenth-of-a-tenth-of-a-tenth structure from a memorised conversion or digit-copying.

constraints: Target age roughly 9–10 (Year 5): recognise and use thousandths and relate them to tenths, hundredths and decimal equivalents.
Build thousandths by subdivision and zooming as actions the child performs, so the recursive tenfold structure is felt, not merely asserted.

A reference chart or diagram with tappable nesting facts and a notation flap can communicate the structure as a reference, but on its own it does not let the child perform the subdivision or the zoom; use it as a reference scaffold alongside, not instead of, hands-on subdivision.

Checkable question formats with distractors assess outcomes and can diagnose errors (whole-number bias, placeholder) but do not by themselves elicit the construction of the nesting; use them to check and route, not as the sole means of teaching the insight.
Always use placeholder cases (25/1000 = 0.025) and comparison cases (0.05 vs 0.005) because faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items.
Address whole-number bias directly by making 'more, smaller parts means each is smaller' visible, rather than by rule assertion.
Treat any physical paper split as a model of the ideal zero-thickness partition: real card has slight thickness and only approximates the mathematical subdivision.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The second listed source (DfE National Curriculum) is marked verified:false in the source row; it is cited only for the Year 5 scope/content statement, not for comparative efficacy.

Self-audit of arithmetic and place value: 25/1000 = 0.025 (2 in hundredths, 5 in thousandths, 0 placeholder in tenths); 25/100 = 0.25; 25/10 = 2.5; 35/1000 = 0.035 — all consistent. The ten-for-one chain 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth, 100 thousandths = 1 tenth, 1000 thousandths = 1 whole is internally consistent. Dividing 0.34–0.35 into ten equal steps puts 0.345 on the fifth mark, i.e. the midpoint and 5 thousandths past 0.34; 0.05 = 50 thousandths and 0.005 = 5 thousandths — consistent.

The original 'conversation' and '3D' fit entries asserted a character/depth 'adds nothing'; these universal-dismissal claims were dropped rather than propagated, since the source ratings do not establish such necessity/impossibility claims. No source establishes that the 2D interactive is superior to any other medium; the medium preference is a pedagogical proposal only.

The source probeDeeper and responseLevels.full extend the ÷10 action to ten-thousandths; this was restored as an action and feedback in the zoom activity so the 'never runs out' claim is enacted, not merely asserted.

Physical paper cut into ten parts is an approximation with thickness; it represents the ideal zero-thickness partition and should be treated as a model of it, not identical to it (noted in the relevant activity, not only here).

assess.poeTask: Before comparing, ask the child to PREDICT which is bigger, one hundredth or one thousandth, and to say WHY. The reason is diagnostic: predicting the thousandth is bigger 'because 1000 beats 100' reveals the whole-number bias. Then split one hundredth into ten and lay a single thousandth beside a hundredth — the thousandth is plainly tiny. Have the child reconcile this with their prediction.
probeDeeper: You wrote 25 thousandths as 0.025. Where does the 2 sit, and where does the 5 sit — and why the zero right after the point?
Which is bigger, 0.05 or 0.005 — and why, when the digits are both 5?
If I split one thousandth into ten equal parts again, what would each tiny piece be called?
Show me where 0.345 goes between 0.34 and 0.35 — how many equal steps are in that gap, and which one is 0.345?
assess.correctAnswer: 10 thousandths in one hundredth; 100 thousandths in one tenth. 25 thousandths = 25/1000 = 0.025; the placeholder zero holds the empty tenths place so the 2 lands in hundredths and the 5 in thousandths (each place a tenth of the one before).

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias: 'a thousandth is bigger than a hundredth because 1000 is bigger than 100'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay one thousandth against one hundredth so the thousandth is visibly tiny; re-establish 'more, smaller parts means each is smaller'. Reteach the tenfold place structure from tenths/hundredths.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a comparison probe (0.05 vs 0.005, or 'which is bigger, a hundredth or a thousandth') picks the thousandth; treats a larger denominator as a larger part.

errorPatterns.pattern: Placeholder error: writes 25 thousandths as 0.25 (or 0.0025) rather than 0.025.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the place-value chart — thousandths is the third place, so 25 occupies hundredths and thousandths with a zero in tenths; contrast 25/100 = 0.25 with 25/1000 = 0.025. Reteach place-fixes-the-value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 0.25 for 25/1000; does not fill the tenths place with a zero.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscoordinates the nesting: says there are 10 thousandths in a tenth (one ×10 step) instead of 100 (two steps).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build it in stages — 10 thousandths make a hundredth, and 10 hundredths make a tenth, so 100 thousandths make a tenth; count on the subdivided line. Reteach composing tenfold steps.
errorPatterns.distractor: There are 10 thousandths in one tenth.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers '10' for thousandths in a tenth; applies a single tenfold step instead of composing two.

responseLevels.gap: Believes a thousandth is bigger than a hundredth, writes 25/1000 as 0.25, or gives 10 thousandths per tenth. No coordinated nesting.
responseLevels.full: Coordinates the nesting (10 thousandths = 1 hundredth, 100 = 1 tenth, 1000 = 1 whole), writes 25/1000 = 0.025 with the placeholder and justifies it, holds that a thousandth is smaller than a hundredth despite 1000 > 100, places 0.345 by zooming between hundredths, and extends the ÷10 action to ten-thousandths.
responseLevels.partial: Can write 0.025 and recite that 1000 thousandths make a whole, but cannot explain the two-step nesting (100 thousandths = 1 tenth) or why the placeholder is needed — lists facts without relating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: How many thousandths are in one hundredth, and how many thousandths are in one tenth? Then write 25 thousandths as a fraction and as a decimal, and tell me why it is written that way.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 'How many thousandths in a tenth' checks whether the child composes two ×10 steps (100) or applies just one (10). Writing 25/1000 exposes the placeholder — a digit-copier writes 0.25. The tier-2 'why' separates a memorised conversion from grasp of the recursive tenth-of-a-tenth-of-a-tenth structure and of a thousandth being smaller than a hundredth despite 1000 > 100.
